description:
TMDO is a team of five: Benjamin Martin, Luca Camaño, Tobias Roncati, Valentin Ribero and Trinidad Cruz. 

Córdoba is one of Argentina’s main farming regions, and we built AgroPixel for the producers and agronomists we see there. We split the work into backend, satellite data and deployment, product and rules engine, and two frontend roles. That way we went from raw NASA data to a working web app at agropixel.earth in 48Hs.
summary:
AgroPixel is a web decision-support tool that helps growers and their agronomists compare crop rotations using NASA data. The user outlines a field on a satellite map and enters the current rotation, priorities (water, soil health, erosion, income) and constraints. AgroPixel then compares that rotation with three alternatives: a winter cover crop (hairy vetch or cereal rye), a commercial winter crop (wheat or barley followed by double-crop soybean), and summer diversification (sorghum or sunflower).

Each option is evaluated against 30 growing seasons of NASA POWER climate data, HLS NDVI at 30 m, NASADEM slope and ESA WorldCover. Results show the trade-offs in water balance, ground cover, nitrogen contribution, erosion risk and income. They are broken down by dry, normal and wet years, with observed frost, heat-stress and dry-sowing frequencies. Growers can also add their own rain-gauge records.

This matters because in Argentina’s Pampas, continuous soybean with long winter fallows degrades soils and increases exposure to drought. AgroPixel makes these trade-offs visible with transparent, traceable rules instead of a black box. It compares and does not recommend: the decision stays with the grower and the agronomist.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

AgroPixel is a web decision-support tool for growers and their agronomists. It answers one question: how would my current crop rotation compare with realistic alternatives on this specific field, given 30 years of climate?

The workflow:

Outline the field. The user draws the field boundary on a satellite basemap, between 1 and 20,000 ha. They can also search for a place or coordinates.

Describe the farm. The user enters:
the current rotation;
priorities from 1 to 5 for water, soil health, erosion and income;
constraints: rainfed, no livestock, limited machinery, excluded crops;
soil texture, and whether the field is prone to waterlogging;
optionally, their own rain-gauge or weather-station records,uploaded as a CSV file.

Analyze. AgroPixel returns a dashboard with three sections:

Map: satellite layers of the field (monthly NDVI with a 12-month timeline, slope, cropland and per-pixel erosion risk). Hovering shows each pixel’s value and source.
Historical climate: the last 30 growing seasons (July–June), colored as dry, normal or wet. Any season can be opened month by month against the 30-year mean.
Rotations: the current rotation side by side with three alternatives, as cards and as a technical table that can be exported to PDF:
A · Winter cover crop: hairy vetch or cereal rye in the winter fallow window.
B · Commercial winter crop: wheat or barley followed by double-crop soybean.
C · Summer diversification: sorghum or sunflower added to the sequence.

Every column has the same five parts: why, evidence, benefits, missing information, and what to check with your agronomist.

Under the hood:

NASA POWER: 30 complete July–June seasons of monthly precipitation and minimum and maximum temperature. From these we compute:
reference evapotranspiration (ET₀, Hargreaves, FAO-56);
the water balance, and terciles of dry, normal and wet years;
frost and heat-stress counts.
Satellite data over the field polygon:
HLS (Landsat + Sentinel-2, 30 m): monthly NDVI and months of low ground cover;
MODIS MOD13Q1: NDVI fallback;
NASADEM: slope and erosion risk;
ESA WorldCover: checks that the polygon is cropland;
MODIS MOD16A3GF: actual evapotranspiration, to cross-check ET₀.

All layers share a common grid of 1 arc-second (~30 m).

Rule engine: fixed agronomic rules score crop water use (crop coefficient × ET₀), nitrogen contribution, crop residue, months of bare soil, erosion risk and a relative income index. A goal fit score weights each criterion by the square of the user’s priority.
Climatological probability: for each rotation’s calendar, it counts the observed frequency of frost on a sensitive crop, sowing with less than half the normal rainfall, and Tmax ≥ 35 °C. It is always shown as a year count, for example “14 of 30 years (47%)”.

What benefits does it have?

Field-specific: satellite data at 30 m over the field’s own boundary, with 30 years of climate behind every number.
Explicit uncertainty: results by dry, normal and wet years, a “climate-sensitive” flag, and event frequencies instead of single averages.
Traceable: every value shows unit, source, period, resolution and confidence. Every text comes from a rule. Gaps are listed under “Missing information”.
Grower data counts more: the grower’s records are compared with NASA over the same seasons and blended into the scores, weighted by years of record (40% to 75%).
Free and open: no login, no stored data, built only on open data.

What is the intended impact?

In Argentina’s Pampas, continuous soybean with long winter fallows depletes soil organic matter, increases water erosion and leaves farms more exposed to drought. Cover crops and more diverse rotations are known to help. Adoption is still limited, because growers need to see the trade-offs on their own field and under their own climate before changing a system that pays today.

AgroPixel puts that evidence on the table in the conversation between grower and agronomist:

how much water a cover crop would use in a dry year;
how many months of bare soil the rotation removes;
how often frost or a dry sowing window would have hurt it.

Next steps:

validate the rules with INTA researchers and local agronomists;
add daily climate data and national weather-station records;
calibrate the engine for other regions, so any farm with NASA coverage can run the same comparison.


How is the project creative?


It compares; it does not prescribe. Most agricultural tools give one answer. AgroPixel never says “best” or “you should”. It shows the four options with the same structure and leaves the decision to the people accountable for it.
Probability as counted years, not a model. Instead of a black-box forecast, it says “this happened in 14 of the last 30 seasons”. Growers and agronomists can verify that and reason with it.
Satellite meets declared rotation. HLS NDVI shows how many months the field was actually bare last season. When that does not match the rotation the user entered, the app flags it for review.
One grid, one truth. Data from 10 m to ~50 km is harmonized onto a single field grid. Every number in the table is the summary of a layer the user can see on the map.
Local knowledge over generic rules: evidence texts cite Argentine field trials (INTA), and the grower’s own rain gauge weighs more than the satellite estimate.
A friendly identity for a technical tool: a pixel-art brand (“AgroPixel”: every pixel of the field counts), with a technical-by-default interface.


What factors did the team consider?


Who the user is: experienced growers and agronomists. The interface is technical by default, with units, sources and confidence on every value. The UI is in Spanish, using local agronomic terms.
Responsibility: a support tool must not replace professional judgment. The notice “Decision-support tool: it does not replace the judgment of the grower or the agronomist” is always visible.
Explainability over sophistication: no AI or machine learning at runtime. Rules, statistics and fixed templates make every result reproducible and auditable.
Scale mismatch: NASA POWER is ~50 km and is labelled “regional context”. MODIS at 250 m mixes the field with its neighbors, so field measurements use HLS at 30 m.
Southern-hemisphere seasons: growing seasons run July–June, not calendar years.
Data caveats: NASA POWER monthly minimum and maximum temperatures are monthly extremes, and the app treats them that way. Cloudy months without a clear HLS scene are reported, not filled in.
Data accessibility: only sources that work without registration and respond in seconds.
Reliability for a live demo:
timeouts on every external source;
partial results when one source fails;
Privacy: no accounts and no stored data. Uploaded records are used only for that analysis.
Scope: the four options, the five parts of each option and the uncertainty by year type were non-negotiable. Everything else could be cut.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?
Frontend: TypeScript, Next.js, React, Leaflet and Recharts, deployed on Vercel at agropixel.earth.
Backend: Python, FastAPI, Pydantic and httpx, deployed on Google Cloud Run.
Data:
NASA POWER API, NASA GIBS (WMTS);
Microsoft Planetary Computer (STAC catalog and polygon statistics) for HLS, MODIS, NASADEM and ESA WorldCover;
Esri World Imagery and Esri geocoding.
Methods: FAO-56 (Hargreaves ET₀), tercile analysis and rule-based scoring.
Quality:
GitHub Actions CI with ruff (linting), pytest (400+ offline tests), gitleaks (secret scanning) and project checks (prescriptive language, domain boundaries);
Claude Code (Anthropic) as a programming assistant, as declared in the SI section.
Design: Figma.
Hardware: none beyond our laptops; everything runs in the cloud.
